row.line: Start feels HARD? We blame oxygen, not you. An exercise science review says it can take 2 to 4 minutes to catch up, longer if you push. And your muscles?

row.line: Not WARM yet. In a small soccer study, warm-ups heated thighs about 3 °C. Rest cooled them... sprints slowed 2.4%. Not yoga. We think it's one reason for sun salutations.

row.line: And your head? In lab tests, thinking during exercise got a bit CLUMSY. For 20 minutes. Then quick choices got a little better. Our advice? Don't judge the start.

row.line: Then the breath. In a small study, marathon runners' breath would LOCK onto their steps within 4 or 5 strides. Beginner runners? Mostly irregular. We count, one movement, one breath.

row.line: Repeat it enough, and a move can go on AUTOPILOT. Done while you think of something else. In finger-tapping scans, the same brain areas still ran it, with less activity.

row.line: Don't grab the wheel. Runners told to WATCH their steps or breath used more oxygen. Same speed. Feeling the body cost nothing extra. We say, learn the count, then feel.

row.line: Then the ZONE, that lost-in-it feeling. 11 runners felt it most at hour one of six. Their front brain got quieter, yet thinking stayed steady.

row.line: And on the mat? In a survey, 127 Ashtanga students felt the zone there more than in another activity. More YEARS, more zone. Our guess? The habit grows it.

row.line: Practice gets CHEAPER, too. In 9 soldiers, sun salutations needed about 30% less oxygen at month 11 than month 3. Small study, no group to compare. Army training may have helped.

row.line: Over a lifetime? Older people who exercised 4 to 5 times a week kept softer, springier hearts. 2 to 3 times did not. A link, not proof. Same time TOMORROW?
